replying_to: Replying to A Step-Wise Weighting Approach for Controllable Text Generation
display_title: Official Review of Paper2317 by Reviewer bQwv

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a step-wise energy-based model (EBM) for controlled text generation (CTG). The authors first derive the step-wise EBM from sequence-level EBM, and then design different keyword-based energy functions for 5 typical scenarios of CTG. The authors also claim their method as a unified framework for CTG, which can be specialized to previous CTG frameworks via a specific energy function design.

Extensive experiments on CTG are conducted based on the automatic metrics of control accuracy, fluency and diversity. Results show that the step-wise EBM can achieve state-of-the-art performance on the tasks of text generation with word / topic / multiple control(s). Also, it is the most efficient method among all the baselines.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
1) As a unified perspective for various CTG frameworks, the proposed step-wise EBM is somewhat novel and interesting. Although this paper only focuses on empirical designs of energy functions, I think the proposed method may be beneficial for further analysis on theoretical properties of various CTG frameworks.
2) Comprehensive and extensive experimental results on automatic metrics show the effectiveness of the step-wise EBM on various CTG tasks. The high computational efficiency of the proposed method is also worth noting.

Weaknesses:
1) In Section 2.2, the derivation from sequence-level EBM to step-wise EBM is questionable. The assumption under Equation 4 and 5 is that $h_{\theta}(c|x_{1:T-1})$ is constant, which is confusing for me. Common attributes to control such as sentiments and topics reflect sentence-level characteristics. So, I can’t understand why previous tokens $x_{1:t-1}$ don’t affect the attribute prediction at the timestep $t$.
2) In Section 2.3, the details on how to choose keywords should be clarified. I wonder how to obtain an external classifier which can predict each word’s sentiment. Furthermore, since the keywords of attributes are still acquired from external attribute classifiers, what is the advantage of utilizing the keywords extracted by classifiers over using classifiers directly?
3) The authors claim the high computational efficiency of the proposed method in Section 1. But I think the difference of efficiency between step-wise EBM and the existing work (such as GeDi) mainly falls into the choice of classifiers (keyword-based classifier vs. neural-network-based classifier) rather than the algorithm itself.
4) This paper lacks human evaluation, which is important for evaluating CTG models and is commonly adopted by related works. The automatic metrics including perplexity, distinct n-grams, and attribute accuracy (from external classifiers) may not correlate well with human judgments.
5) The choice of base models may cause an unfair comparison. From Section 3, the authors choose GPT-2 small as the base LM, which is different from several baselines. From Table 3, the authors explain that CTRL and DAPT perform better because they use GPT-2 large as the base LM. But in my view, the authors should make a fair comparison at least based on the same base LM to demonstrate the effectiveness of their own methods. Also, in Section 3.5, the computational efficiency is strongly affected by the model size. From Table 6, I feel that the superior efficiency of the proposed model mainly comes from the smaller base LM rather than the proposed method (i.e. step-wise EBM).
6) I have a minor concern about the experiment. In Table 4, I see the perplexity of GPT-3 models is missing. The reason should be further clarified.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Strengths:
1) A somewhat novel and interesting EBM framework for CTG tasks
2) Strong performance on automatic metrics

Weaknesses:
1) Questionable assumptions
2) Lack of human evaluation
3) Unfair experimental setups about base LMs

display_title: Clarification on keyword selection, efficiency comparisons, and perplexity scores for methods using GPT-3

content.title: Clarification on keyword selection, efficiency comparisons, and perplexity scores for methods using GPT-3
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for recognizing the main contributions of our work. We addressed your confusion on the assumptions around Eqs. 4 and 5. We have also added human evaluation results. Below, we answer your specific questions.

**How to obtain external classifier and its advantage of using external classifier instead of directly using it during generation**

There are many ways to choose keywords. For some of the instantiations of our energy function, e.g., for sentiment control, the procedure goes as follows. First, we select an external classifier, which in our case is the Huggingface sentiment classification pipeline. Second, we select a threshold for positive and negative sentiment, respectively. Third, we loop through each word/token in the base LM’s vocabulary. If the word/token falls within the threshold for positive (negative) sentiment, we add it to the keyword list associated with positive (negative) sentiment. For detoxification, the procedure is almost identical to sentiment control, except that here, we use the toxicity classifier from Perspective AI. We realize that we introduced these classifiers in the experiment section (Section 3, “Metrics”) but did not mention them earlier when we discussed keyword selection. We have added the keyword selection details to Supplementary Material C.1.

**Unfair efficiency comparison due to base LM**

We agree that the comparison can be confusing because the base LM in each method is different. However, our method is still superior in terms of computation regardless of model size. The improvement in efficiency is because our method does not involve any external model during generation instead of difference in model sizes. We have updated Table 6 to explicitly compare different base LM sizes. The results clearly show that, even for different model sizes, our method is still more efficient than baselines. We hope that Table 6 is now a fair comparison and clears your concern.

**Missing PPL score for GPT-3 generation**

We have added the perplexity scores for methods using GPT-3 as the base LM to Table 4. Note that, for these methods, we use OpenAI’s GPT-3 for perplexity computation to match with the base LM. For all other CTG methods, we use GPT-2 for perplexity computation.

content.title: Question about independence assumption
content.comment: I have read the response from the authors and I'm satisfied about most parts. However, I'm still confused about the independence assumption in Section 2.2, which is the core of deriving step-wise EBM. In my view, $p_{\theta}(c|x_{1:t-1})=p(c)$ means that the control attribute $c$ is independent with all the prefixes of the text sequence $x$. But obviously the attribute of different prefixes could be different.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposed a general framework for controllable text generation tasks, which approximates the sentence-level energy-based model to a product of step-wise ones and thus enjoys high training efficiency. Some energy functions are instantiated for different controllable signals and experiments. Experiments validate the performance of effectiveness and efficiency over some competitive methods.
content.main_review:
First, it is meaningful to approximate the sentence-level EGM to step-wise EGM. However, I am not very clear why some approximations. In Eq.4, I think for different x’s, h(c|x) should not be a constant. Why here can make such assumption? How the approximation of using top-k sampling used in training? Especially when the target x_t^{(t)} has not yet been included in top k in the current iteration?

Second and also my major concern is about the energy function design. It seems not a good choice to pre-classify each word into certain sentiment or toxicity without a context. For example, if the previous generated text contains a negation such as “not”, “doesn’t”, the energy function will function in a wrong way? Also, I notice that in the experiment part of 3.4，the considered topics have no overlapping topic keywords. What would happen if the topics have overlapped keywords?

For the experimental results, considering that the major advantage of this method is its high efficiency, I am ok with the current results that the proposed model does not outperform some methods on most of the compared controllable generation tasks.

display_title: Clarification on training, top-k sampling, and compositions of controls

content.title: Clarification on training, top-k sampling, and compositions of controls
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for recognizing the value of approximating sequence-level EBM as step-wise EBM. We address some of your questions, in particular, assumptions and complex control cases, in the general reply above. Below, we clarify your specific questions.

**Top-k sampling and training**

There is no training involved in our work; top-k is strictly used during generation. There are certainly cases where the target word does not appear in the top-k most probable words/tokens at a given time step during generation. Fortunately, our energy function is specifically designed in such a way that the target word(s) will eventually (or highly likely) appear in the top-k most probable words/tokens and thus in the generated text. This is achieved by strategically reweighing the probability of each word at each generation step, which is the core idea of our energy function design. Experiments consistently demonstrate that our method can achieve perfect or highly competitive control satisfaction.

**What happens if we use topics with overlapping keyword lists?**

We did not perform an experiment with topics containing overlapping keywords because it is a simpler case. This is because, if a single work/token that belongs to both topics is generated during CTG, we would consider this generated sample a successful satisfaction of both topics. This would be a simpler case because both topics are satisfied simultaneously with just one work/token. We chose the more difficult case in which topics have non-overlapping words/tokens, which implies that a CTG method needs to generate at least two words/tokens, one for each topic, in order to satisfy both topics.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2317 by Reviewer Cf77
display_title: Our framework is more than incremental

content.title: Our framework is more than incremental
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the constructive feedback, which has helped us improve the clarity and presentation of our draft. We have clarified on the assumptions related to Eq. 5 and provided examples that demonstrate the reliability of our approach in our general reply above. We have also added human evaluation experiments, per your suggestion. Below, we address your specific questions.

**The framework is incremental because it is only an extension of auto-regressive LMs.**

We respectfully disagree with the reviewer’s claim that our work is incremental because **“extending auto-regressive LMs” for the task of CTG is nontrivial**. Indeed, this is a rather challenging task, which is why a lot of well-cited literature in NLP is devoted to studying this problem, i.e., how to extend existing LMs to generate texts that satisfy certain attributes. Furthermore, our work differentiates from existing literature in that 1) we provide a general framework that unifies many existing approaches and 2) we design a simple albeit efficient and effective energy function under our framework that consistently demonstrates strong performance across a variety of CTG tasks. Therefore, we believe that our work provides new insights, offers new CTG approaches, demonstrates comprehensive and competitive results, and thus is much more than “incremental in nature and lacks novelty which is only an extension to the probability function of the vanilla auto-regressive LMs”. 

**Samples are too few**

We actually used way more than 100 samples for each experiment. For example, The word and topic control experiment each involves 900 generated samples per method (100 for each control word or topic and we used 9 control words and 9 control topics, respectively). The sentiment control experiment involves 1200 generated samples per method (100 for each prompt for each sentiment and we use 6 prompts). The Detoxification experiment involves 2000 generated samples per method (10 for each prompt and we use 100 toxic and 100 non-toxic prompts). The experiment on composition of controls involves 1500 generated samples per method. All the above info is clearly stated at the beginning of each experiment subsection. In addition, we actually use more samples for evaluation than many baseline methods. In comparison, GeDi uses 100 samples; PPLM uses 420 samples; Fudge uses 154 samples; PnB uses 100 samples. The number of samples in our work is only shadowed by DExperts. Although it is always good to use more samples in the evaluation, considering the breadth of our evaluation, both in terms of the number of tasks and the number of baselines under comparison, we believe the number of samples in our experiment sufficiently substantiates the results and conclusions in the paper.

display_title: Official Review of Paper2317 by Reviewer yvm1

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a method of controllable text generation where the goal is to generate text from a language model given an attribute such as a specific topic, sentiment, or toxicity. Presented as a step-wise approximation of a previously proposed EBM-based method [1], the method works by modifying the output softmax distribution at each decoding step of the language model to increase or decrease the influence of the desired attribute. The energy functions for desired controls are represented using the presence or absence of predefined keywords in the vocabulary. With this setup, the authors show improvements over several baselines on metrics such as fluency, diversity, and control on tasks of controlling topic, sentiment, and reducing toxicity in the outputs and their combinations. The authors also show that this formulation subsumes many related papers in this area which also modify output probabilities to enforce control.
content.main_review:
Strengths: 
1. The presented solution is quite simple and the improvements obtained by using only keyword presence or absence-based controls are impressive especially compared to earlier work which uses more sophisticated methods based on classifiers or language models. 

2. The proposed approach is fast and has little overhead.

Weaknesses:

1. The motivation for the EBM formulation is not very clear. Although many papers (as the authors describe in the appendix) can be subsumed under this framework, it is not clear what insight it offers since it does not particularly give us a new way of designing constraints.

2. "> certain words carry important attribute-sensitive information" 
The constraints the author consider are keyword-based [1]. While this might work for cases such as topic or even sentiment. For more nuanced attributes not necessarily satisfied using keywords only or sentence-level attributes that cannot be measured just using the generated prefix (such as poetry generation, formality, etc), it's not clear how to define energy functions except for using classifiers or LMs which prior work like FUDGE or DExperts already does. How does this work differentiate from similar prior work in that case?

Some questions/suggestions:
1. Since the evaluation is quite subjective, it could benefit from some human evaluation to make the results more convincing.
2. For measuring control for sentiment/toxicity the authors report the average probability of the desired attribute measured by the classifiers whereas prior work reports the accuracy of the desired attribute. If the generated text is say, non-toxic, as predicted by the classifier, does it matter if the probability was 0.9 or 0.6 (especially considering the classifiers may not be well-calibrated)?

Some missing citations: 
[1] NeuroLogic Decoding: (Un)supervised Neural Text Generation with Predicate Logic Constraints (https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.12884)
[2] CoCon: A Self-Supervised Approach for Controlled Text Generation (https://openreview.net/forum?id=VD_ozqvBy4W)
content.summary_of_the_review: The presented approach on controllable text generation while showing improvements on keyword-based controls like topic or sentiment, does not offer any new insights in its formulation as an energy-based model. Furthermore, it's not clear how keyword-based controls are flexible enough or can be extended to setups other than the ones presented in the paper.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2317 by Reviewer yvm1
display_title: Clarifications on the usefulness of our approach and how it differentiates from existing methods

content.title: Clarifications on the usefulness of our approach and how it differentiates from existing methods
content.comment:
We appreciate the reviewer for recognizing the simplicity, effectiveness, and efficiency of our approach. Below, we address your questions and concerns. 


**Usefulness of the EBM formulation**

Our formulation offers a new way to design an energy function in the form of Eq. 10. This is a very general class of energy functions and can take many different forms, e.g., the parameters $\lambda$’s and $\phi$’s can be dependent on timesteps, previous generations and even involve external models. In this work, we explored in Sec. 3 one of the many possible instantiations of this class of energy functions, which highlights its simplicity, efficiency, and effectiveness.


**Differentiation between our method and classifier-based CTG methods**

Our energy function takes a “classifier-free” design, which is the main difference between our approach and existing CTG methods that mostly involve external models in addition to the base generative LM. While prior work glossed over simple methods that contain no external classifiers, we show that carefully designed energy functions without using these external models can achieve similar or even better results compared to existing CTG approaches. We agree that our method’s weakness lies in its limitation to generate texts with subtle and nuanced forms of attributes. However, for the CTG tasks we consider in this work, which are commonly studied in literature, we demonstrate strongly competitive performance.


**Human evaluation**

We agree that human evaluation is beneficial and have performed additional human evaluation. 


**Evaluation metric for sentiment controlled generation**

We believe as long as the metric is the same across all methods under comparison, we have a fair comparison, which is what we did for all our experiments. Regarding using probabilities instead of class labels: first, the perspective API does not provide a class label so we have to use its returned toxicity probability. Second, in the sentiment analysis, we actually did report in the paper the percentage of the desired class instead of class confidence (although we have recorded both metrics). We have clarified this in the “Metrics” paragraph before Section 3.1.


**Additional references**

Thanks for the pointers. We actually have cited the second paper you referred us to; this has been cited in the “Related Work” section, now in Supplementary Material B. We have now included the first reference you mentioned in our revised draft.

content.title: General reply to reviewers
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback. We have since integrated these suggestions into a revised draft where we marked the changes in violet color. We have also performed additional experiments and analyses per the reviewers' requests. Here, we address the common concerns shared among all four reviewers. 

 

**On novelty**

Reviewers suggest that the work lacks novelty because our framework offers no new insights, and our energy function design is too simplistic and straightforward. We emphasize that the core value of the paper lies in 
1. We provide a unified perspective that generalizes many existing step-wise EBM methods through the lens of energy functions that operate at every generation step. We believe abstracting individual methods into a unified framework is in itself an interesting finding. In addition to generalizing various existing methods, our framework also provides a recipe for flexible designs of new CTG methods in the form of energy function designs. 
1. We develop a class of energy functions that applies to a range of CTG tasks. Despite its simplicity, our energy function is intuitive, easy to adjust, and at the same time, surprisingly efficient and effective. We show that, without the added complexities, our method can achieve performance on-par with more sophisticated techniques. This simplicity and effectiveness is in itself another interesting finding, suggesting that for many CTG tasks, we do not need complex methods to achieve good performance. 
   
 
  
**On limitation of our method for complex and nuanced control attributes**

Our method certainly cannot handle all cases, such as complex or subtle sentiments that Reviewers brought out. However, this limitation does not imply that our method cannot successfully perform CTG, as evidenced by the strong empirical performance throughout our experiments. The reviewers unanimously point to the double negation example, e.g., "not bad," and suggest that our method will not handle this case. However, empirically, it seems that our method simply avoids generating texts with double negation instead of generating texts with the wrong sentiment. For example, by manually inspecting all 600 samples generated by our approach with "positive sentiment" as the control, only 10 samples contain the word "not," and most of them are neutral or positive in sentiment. Below are 3 examples:

1. "The pizza lovers love to eat pizza, and this amazing treat won't stay up well for long. Fortunately, you won't need much care for pizza making! Well, not exactly. You'll be surprised by"
1. "You may not believe you can make good food with salt, salt, salt. Yes, salt is a great food! The salt goes great with sweet treats. The salt does give you extra energy!"
1. "You will not be able to connect to this site until you log in! You will have to go to your account settings and create something unique. Please confirm your account information."

We will happily supply more examples upon reviewers' request. 

As for more complex CTG cases such as poetry or formality, these are not very commonly studied in the existing literature and are more challenging cases that require more careful energy function designs. Therefore, we defer the investigation of these more challenging CTG cases to future work but note that for the CTG cases we consider in the present work, our method is highly competitive and efficient, despite its simplicity.

 

**On the assumptions in Eqs. 4 and 5 in the original draft**

The reviewers raise concerns about the validity of assumptions in Eq. 4 and 5 in the original draft. The census seems to be that one cannot assume $h_\theta$ to be a constant. We recognize the derivation in our original draft may be confusing. Therefore, we have rewritten and reorganized part of Section 2.2, explicitly elaborated on the assumptions (independence and constant time assumptions) that our approximation relies on, and introduced our step-wise EBM framework with more clarity. Please refer to the revised Section 2.2 for more details, particularly those texts marked in violet. 

 

**On human evaluation**

We heed the reviewers' suggestions and performed human evaluations for CTG scenarios, including sentiment-controlled generation and detoxification where the control attribute can be subtle and nuanced and automatic evaluations alone may be insufficient. Human evaluation results corroborate with automatic evaluation metrics and demonstrate our method's competitiveness in achieving high language quality and satisfying control compared to strong baselines. Human evaluation results are now available in Tables 3 and 4. Details of the evaluation setup are available in Supplementary Material C.3.
